How to Introduce Your Indoorsy Friend to the Outdoors

By Corey Buhay August 12, 2014

We all have that one friend who considers a hotel with spotty Wi-Fi "roughing it." Maybe they come up with excuses every time you invite them camping, or they blanch at the idea of sleeping without a mattress. Whatever the reason, their indoor comfort zone has kept them from experiencing the magic of the outdoors.

But here's the secret: almost everyone can become an outdoor enthusiast with the right introduction. The key is starting small, staying patient, and making the first experience as enjoyable as possible.

1. Start with a Day Trip

Don't jump straight to a week-long backpacking expedition. Instead, propose a casual day hike at a local park or nature area. Keep the distance manageable—under five miles—and choose a trail with a clear payoff, like a waterfall or scenic overlook.

Day trips remove the anxiety of overnight sleeping arrangements, and they give your friend the freedom to bail if things aren't going well (though they rarely do).

2. Front-Load the Comfort

Bring snacks. Lots of them. The quickest way to win over a reluctant outdoor companion is with good food. Trail mix, fresh fruit, sandwiches, or even a thermos of hot coffee can transform a challenging hike into a pleasant picnic with a scenic walk attached.

If you're camping, consider starting with a car-camping trip rather than backpacking. Car camping lets you bring a real sleeping pad, a camp chair, and more food than you can carry on your back.

3. Gear Up Thoughtfully

Nothing dampens outdoor enthusiasm faster than blisters from bad boots or hypothermia from inadequate layers. Before the trip, help your friend borrow or rent appropriate gear. REI's rental program is a great way to try gear before buying.

The basics they'll need:

  • Broken-in hiking boots or trail shoes
  • Moisture-wicking base layers
  • A waterproof jacket
  • A daypack with enough room for water, snacks, and a first-aid kit
  • Sunscreen and insect repellent

4. Let Them Set the Pace

Resist the urge to barrel ahead on the trail. Match your pace to your friend's comfort level and be willing to take breaks. The goal for this first trip isn't to conquer miles — it's to help them fall in love with being outside.

Point out interesting things along the way: wildflowers, bird calls, unusual rock formations. Help them see the outdoors as endlessly fascinating rather than a landscape to be endured.

5. Have a Backup Plan

Weather happens. Unexpected rain or heat can turn a pleasant outing into a miserable slog. Check the forecast beforehand and have a contingency plan — a different trail, an alternate activity, or even just a nearby café where you can warm up and regroup.

Flexibility goes a long way toward ensuring a good first outdoor experience.

The Long Game

Converting an indoorsy friend to an outdoor enthusiast rarely happens in one trip. It's a gradual process of building positive associations with being outside. Keep the pressure low, celebrate small victories, and let their curiosity grow at its own pace.

Before long, you might find yourself struggling to keep up with your once-reluctant hiking partner.
